item.title: TISI Sangam election didn't go ahead, interim committee to oversee affairs
item.description: The TISI Sangam election did not go ahead as scheduled today at Sangam College in Nadi, with National President Parveen Bala confirming that an Interim Committee has been nominated to oversee the organisation’s affairs for now. Bala and fellow presidential candidate Damend Gounder have nominated the Interim Committee, and a Council of Management meeting will be held soon to provide further directi
item.content:encoded:
The TISI Sangam election did not go ahead as scheduled today at Sangam College in Nadi, with National President Parveen Bala confirming that an Interim Committee has been nominated to oversee the organisation’s affairs for now.

Bala and fellow presidential candidate Damend Gounder have nominated the Interim Committee, and a Council of Management meeting will be held soon to provide further direction.

When questioned about the commotion during the election and Annual General Meeting, Bala told fijivillage News that heated arguments can be expected during a large gathering, but everything was under control.

Insert: Floor given to members 27th Sept

Some of the members publicly said they want the elections to go ahead.

Following a closed-door meeting, Bala and Gounder agreed to serve as co-chairs of the Interim Committee, with each expected to appoint seven members as interim executives.

The other presidential candidate, Dorsami Naidu, will also be included in the Interim Committee.

Earlier today, TISI Sangam members had been pushing for the elections to proceed as scheduled and not be delayed.

item.title: Mother recalls fear, sacrifice and joy as son beats blood cancer
item.description: Nazia Ali, mother of 14-year-old Hazrat Ali, remembers the devastation she felt 12 years ago when doctors first told her that her two-year-old son had blood cancer. Sharing her family’s experience during Gold September, which raises awareness about childhood cancer, Ali says her son’s symptoms included unexplained pain in his leg and a fever.
item.content:encoded:
Nazia Ali, mother of 14-year-old Hazrat Ali, remembers the devastation she felt 12 years ago when doctors first told her that her two-year-old son had blood cancer.

Sharing her family’s experience during Gold September, which raises awareness about childhood cancer, Ali says her son’s symptoms included unexplained pain in his leg and a fever.

She says her son is now 14 years old, healthy and cancer-free, but she still remembers how difficult it was to accept the diagnosis.

Ali says there is also a misconception that blood cancer only affects children who have a family history of the disease, stressing that this is not necessarily the case.

She says Hazrat began chemotherapy, she tried to make the frightening experience easier for him by telling him the treatment would turn him into a superhero.

However, behind those words of encouragement, Ali says she was scared after doctors told the family her son had a 50-50 chance.

She says instead of focusing on the possibility of losing him, she placed her faith in the positive 50 percent and continued to hope that he would recover.

Ali says she was also frightened when doctors warned that there was a high possibility of the cancer returning.

As a teacher, Ali took leave without pay so she could care for her son throughout his three years of treatment , most of which was carried out in Fiji.

After years of chemotherapy, uncertainty and sacrifice, the mother says one of the happiest moments for the family came when they were finally told that Hazrat was cancer-free.

item.title: Paddle for Hope team completes 500km journey around Viti Levu
item.description: For 28 days and more than 500 kilometres around Viti Levu, Reverend James Bhagwan and Graham Taylor paddled with one central message: what is thrown on land eventually finds its way to the ocean. The two paddlers, and their team, have now completed their journey around Fiji's main island and were welcomed at the USP foreshore this afternoon, where they reflected on the challenges they faced along
item.content:encoded:
For 28 days and more than 500 kilometres around Viti Levu, Reverend James Bhagwan and Graham Taylor paddled with one central message: what is thrown on land eventually finds its way to the ocean.

The two paddlers, and their team, have now completed their journey around Fiji's main island and were welcomed at the USP foreshore this afternoon, where they reflected on the challenges they faced along the way and the communities they met.

Taylor says the journey was far from easy, with illness and challenging weather conditions testing the paddlers during the 28-day journey.

He says one of the team members was admitted to hospital with flu-like symptoms the night before they left Suva, while he later became ill himself.

Taylor says there was a point when he considered abandoning the journey after spending a night feeling unwell.

He says medication helped him recover enough to continue the following day.

The weather also presented major challenges, particularly on the second day of the journey from Muaivuso to Togoru.

Taylor says what was expected to be a four-hour journey took six hours, with the team relying on their support crew on land when they eventually arrived.

He says despite the physical challenges, encounters with marine life became some of the highlights of the journey.

Taylor says during one of the most difficult stretches, he and Reverend Bhagwan questioned whether they should continue.

He says seeing turtles and birds along the way gave them another reason to keep paddling.

Taylor says the journey was not only about the paddlers, but also about the environment and the communities they visited.

He thanked villages along the route for welcoming the team, providing hot meals and sharing their experiences and concerns .

Taylor says the team heard a number of messages from communities that they will carry forward, including needs identified during their visits.

He also acknowledged the support crew, who he says were up before dawn each morning to prepare meals and ensure the paddlers were ready for the day.

Permanent Secretary for Environment and Climate Change Dr Sivendra Michael says the journey was more than a paddle, with the team engaging with communities at various stops around Viti Levu.

Michael says the team visited places including Togoru, Navua and Galoa, where they cleaned beaches, sorted waste, worshipped and took part in talanoa sessions.

He says the message from the journey was simple, protecting the oceans starts with what people do in their own homes and villages.

Michael says Paddle for Hope has also taken the pre-COP31 message to communities, highlighting the importance of protecting villages, reefs and rivers.

He says the completion of the journey demonstrates that collective action, one paddle stroke and one household at a time, can help reduce the use of single-use plastics and protect Fiji's oceans.

item.title: Man stabbed at Blacktown Train Station in Western Sydney
item.description: Navitalai Naivalurua · 27/09/2026 A man was rushed to hospital after being stabbed at a train station in Western Sydney.
item.content:encoded:
Navitalai Naivalurua · 27/09/2026

A man was rushed to hospital after being stabbed at a train station in Western Sydney.

Emergency services received reports of an assault at Blacktown Train Station.

Police arrived soon after and found a man, believed to be in his 30s, with a stab wound to his arm.

He was treated by paramedics before being taken to hospital in a stable condition.

Police were told the man was involved in an altercation with another man who was armed with a knife, with the incident spreading from the platform onto the tracks.

The other man left the station before police arrived.

Footage from the scene shows officers speaking to several people at the station and searching around a stopped train.

item.title: Dreaming of medicine since childhood: Brian Malani’s journey to becoming a Doctor
item.description: After watching films as a child, Brian Malani was inspired to pursue his childhood dream of becoming a doctor, driven by the desire to help people in a medical facility. Malani, who hails from Nabukadra in Ra and shares maternal links to Tailevu, completed his secondary school at Marist Brothers High School in 2008.
item.content:encoded:
After watching films as a child, Brian Malani was inspired to pursue his childhood dream of becoming a doctor, driven by the desire to help people in a medical facility.

Malani, who hails from Nabukadra in Ra and shares maternal links to Tailevu, completed his secondary school at Marist Brothers High School in 2008.

At 19 years old, he was later offered a scholarship to study medicine in China.

Malani says he first studied the Chinese language at Tongji University before pursuing medicine at Southeast University.

He says one of the challenges he faced was learning Chinese and Mandarin within a short period of 10 months, which was an uphill battle for him.

Malani recalls attending his first class at the university, where he had hoped to meet other Pacific Islanders and fellow Fijians . However, he was the only Fijian in a class dominated by Chinese students, along with students from other countries.

The RFMF captain says learning basic conversations was critical, and he was fortunate to study alongside other foreign students, which made the transition easier.

He says he kept the students motivated by encouraging them to struggle together.

This inspired the group to learn the language within the 10-month period.

Malani says that after completing the 10 months of language study, the students were separated according to their chosen fields of study, including law, fashion and medicine.

He says his first experience in the classroom was an unforgettable one as he had to find ways to fit into a class where the students did not understand English and spoke only Mandarin.

Despite the language barrier, he tried his best to speak and greet his classmates.

Insert: Malani on first day of class 26th Sep

Malani says he studied medicine for six years in China before graduating and returning to Fiji, where he spent some time at Colonial War Memorial Hospital and worked alongside former Health Minister Dr Iferemi Waqainabete.

He says working at CWM Hospital presented another challenge because he had studied medicine entirely in Chinese.

Hearing medical terms in English meant he had to translate them into Chinese in order to understand them.

Malani says that after two years of internship, he gradually became familiar with the system and found himself back on familiar ground.

He says he joined the Republic of Fiji Military Forces in 2019 and later travelled to Iraq, where he served his duty as a medical doctor for the army.

When asked about his biggest motivation, Malani says his parents, particularly his mother, and his siblings were his greatest source of hope.

They encouraged him to keep praying, regardless of the challenges he faced.

He says he found comfort in talking to his mother.

Malani recalls opening his books and seeing everything written in Chinese.

At times, he would ask himself what he was doing there, but thoughts of his family pus hed him to persevere and complete his studies.

His message to children is to stay away from drugs, continue to trust in the Lord and listen to their parents.

Malani is challenging children across Fiji to pursue their dreams, value education and leave the rest in the hands of the Lord.

item.title: Online abuse can push women out of public and political life – Peterson
item.description: Speaking during a panel discussion on technology-facilitated gender-based violence in political life, National Coordinator for the Fijian National Action Plan to Prevent Violence Against Women and Girls, Laisani Peterson says online abuse can silence women, damage their reputation and create fear about participating in public life. She says violence against women online should not be treated separ
item.content:encoded:
Speaking during a panel discussion on technology-facilitated gender-based violence in political life, National Coordinator for the Fijian National Action Plan to Prevent Violence Against Women and Girls, Laisani Peterson says online abuse can silence women, damage their reputation and create fear about participating in public life.

She says violence against women online should not be treated separately from violence experienced offline, as both can be linked to gender inequality, power imbalances and harmful social attitudes.

Peterson says women should be able to speak, lead, campaign and participate in public and political life without fear of abuse or retaliation.

She says addressing technology-facilitated gender-based violence should not be left to survivors to address alone.

Peterson says Government, political parties, law enforcement agencies, civil society organisations, communities and online platforms all have a responsibility to respond.

She says political parties should have clear codes of conduct, condemn online abuse and support women candidates and leaders who are targeted.

Peterson says parties should also ensure their members and supporters are not contributing to harassment, misinformation or intimidation.

She says clear reporting processes and support services are needed for survivors, while online platforms should remove harmful content quickly and cooperate with authorities.

Peterson says the Online Safety Commission has also become a signatory to Fiji's revised service delivery protocol, providing another avenue for people to report online harm through its toll-free number 1548.

She says preventing technology-facilitated gender-based violence is not only about online safety, but also about ensuring women and girls can participate in public life safely and confidently.
